title: Raindrops aren’t teardrop-shaped: big ones look like hamburger buns
body: The pointy-topped drop on every weather icon doesn’t exist. The smallest drops are pulled into near-perfect spheres by surface tension. As drops grow, air resistance pushing up on the bottom flattens them into a **hamburger-bun shape**, and the very largest stretch into something like a parachute before the air tears them into smaller drops. Raindrops range from about 0.1 to 9 mm across, and larger drops fall faster: a 0.5 mm drizzle drop lands at about 2 m/s, a 5 mm drop at around 9 m/s.

slides.alt: A crossed-out teardrop, then four real raindrop shapes in a row from small to very large: a sphere, a slightly flattened blob, a hamburger-bun shape flat underneath, and a parachute shape hollow underneath. Arrows show air pushing up on the big ones.
slides.caption: Small drops are spheres; big ones flatten underneath, then split.

left.label: Icon
left.text: A teardrop with a pointed top, trailing behind as it falls.

right.label: Reality
right.text: Round when small, flattened underneath when large, and never pointed. Air pushes up on the bottom while surface tension holds the top.

slides.label: how fast a 5 mm raindrop hits the ground
slides.text: A 0.5 mm drizzle drop lands at about 2 m/s. Bigger drops have more weight for their drag, so they fall faster.

slides.question: How wide was the biggest raindrop ever recorded?
slides.explanation: About 10 mm. Drops have a tendency to break up as they grow, so they rarely get much bigger than that.
